la:adj:ieiunus.html:
jējūnus, a, um, adj.
kindr. to Sanscr. yam, refrenare, cohibere; intens. yanyam, Bopp. Gloss. p. 276, a
,
fasting, hungry, abstinent, not partaking of food.
Lit.: in scenam qui jejunus venerit,: sic expletur jejuna cupido,hunger,; so, jejuna aviditas,: misera ac jejuna plebecula,: cum quidem biduum ita jejunus fuissem, ut, etc.,: canis,: jejuna fessaque corpora,.—Of inanimate things: lupus jejunis dentibus acer,: Cerberus jejuno sono,with hungry howlings,tam jejuna fames?so extreme,: pullus ad quem volat mater jejuna,: odium,i. e. on an empty stomach,: saliva,fasting spittle,.—
Thirsty: vilem jejunae saepe negavit aquam, (4, 14), 18.—
Transf.
Dry, barren, unproductive: corpora suco jejuna,: ager,: glarea,: pars jejunior humi,.—
Scanty, insignificant in quantity: summaque jejunā sanie infuscatur arena,.—
Trop.
Poor, barren, powerless: ut quosdam nimis jejuno animo et angusto monerem uti, etc.,: pusillus animus atque ipsā malevolentiā jejunus atque inanis,.—
Insignificant, trifling, contemptible, mean, low: solivaga cognitio et jejuna,: frigida et jejuna calumnia,: jejunum hoc nescio quid et contemnendum,: aliquid humile et jejunum,.—
Of speech, meagre, dry, feeble, spiritless: si quis aut Antonium jejuniorem, aut Crassum fuisse pleniorem putet,: Theodorus, in arte subtilior, in orationibus jejunior,.—With gen., : concertatio verborum,; ; —
Destitute of, without, deprived of: divitiarum avidi ac jejuni,: pecunia,.—Adv.: jējūnē, meagrely, dryly, jejunely, without ornament or spirit: jejune et exiliter disputare,; ; : agere,.—Comp.: dicere jejunius,; .

la:noun:ieiunium.html:
jējūnĭum, ii, n.
id.
,
a fast-day, fast.
Lit.: jejunium Cereri instituere,: illos longa domant inopi jejunia victu,: solvere,: ponere,: jejunia indicere,: servare,: jejunio aegrum vexare,.—
Transf.
Hunger: in vacuis spargit jejunia venis,: jejunia pascere,: sedare,: placare voracis jejunia ventris,.—Poet.: jejunia undae,thirst,.—
Leanness, poorness: invalidique patrum referant jejunia nati,.—
Barrenness, unproductiveness: macram ac tenuem terram jejunio laborare,.

senses: the seat of the passions and affections
la:noun:iecur.html:
jĕcur (jŏcur, Sillig.
N. cr.), jecŏris, jĕcĭnŏris, and jĕcĭnŏris, n.
kindred to Sanscr. yakrit, jecur, and Gr. ἧπαρ
, the liver.—Lit.: cerebrum, cor, pulmones, jecur: haec enim sunt domicilia vitae,: portae jecoris,: jecorum,: caput jecoris,: alterius quoque visceris morbus id est jocinoris, etc.,.—The goose's liver was considered a delicacy, ; ; ; . So, too, that of swine, .—
Esp. as the seat of the soul and affections: non ancilla tuum jecur ulceret ulla puerve,: fervens difficili bile tumet jecur,: quanta siccum jecur ardeat ira,: rabie jecur incendente feruntur,.—As the seat of the understanding: en cor Zenodoti, en jecur Cratetis, Bibacul. ap. .

jējūno, 1, v. n.
id.
,
